entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To think of an idea, plan, answer or solution, especially when one is needed.
entries.usage: One of the most common phrasal verbs in conversation and at work: *come up with an idea, a plan, a name, an excuse*. It is inseparable: the object always follows *with*, even a pronoun (*Who came up with this?*). It can also mean find money that you need: *come up with the rent*.
entries.pattern: come up with + idea / plan / name / solution / excuse
examples: We need a name for the new puppy; can anyone **come up with** something better than Max?
The engineers **came up with** a clever fix that cut the battery's charging time in half.
He always **comes up with** some excuse to leave family parties early.

drill.sentence: Our budget was cut in half, so we had to {{come up with}} a cheaper way to run the summer camp.
drill.hint: produce, as a new idea (three words; not *think of* or *figure out*)

entries.related: *think of* — plainer, often for one quick idea; *figure out* — solve by thinking; *dream up* — invent something unusual or unrealistic.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To understand or solve something by thinking about it carefully, often after some time or effort.
entries.usage: Extremely common in American speech, often with a question word: *figure out how / why / what …*. It is separable: a noun can go before or after *out*, but a pronoun must go in the middle (*figure it out*). It also works for people you do not understand: *I can't figure her out.*
entries.pattern: figure out + how / why / what …; figure it out
examples: It took me twenty minutes to **figure out** how to turn on the shower in the hotel.
I've known him for ten years, and I still can't **figure him out**.
Doctors are still trying to **figure out** what caused the rash.

drill.sentence: The instructions were only in Swedish, so we had to {{figure out}} how to build the bookcase from the pictures.
drill.hint: understand by thinking hard (not *work out*)

mistake.wrong: Don't worry, I'll figure out it later.
mistake.right: Don't worry, I'll figure it out later.
mistake.why: With a separable phrasal verb, a pronoun object must go between the verb and the particle.

entries.related: *work out* — the same, more common in British English; *find out* — learn a fact, often by asking or checking; *make sense of* — understand something confusing.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To finally be in a place, state or situation, usually one you did not plan or expect.
entries.usage: Extremely common in storytelling and conversation. It is followed by *-ing* (*we ended up walking*), by a place or *with* + noun (*ended up in Ohio*, *ended up with a cold*), or by an adjective or noun (*ended up broke*, *ended up friends*). It has no direct object.
entries.pattern: end up + -ing / in + place / with + noun / adjective
examples: We meant to stay for one drink, but we **ended up** dancing until two in the morning.
He moved to New York to be an actor and **ended up** running a restaurant.
If you don't fix that leak, you'll **end up** with a huge water bill.

drill.sentence: Our flight was canceled, so we {{ended up}} spending the night on the airport floor.
drill.hint: found ourselves, without planning it (not *wound up*)

mistake.wrong: There were no taxis, so we ended up to walk home.
mistake.right: There were no taxis, so we ended up walking home.
mistake.why: *End up* is followed by *-ing*, not by *to* + verb.

entries.related: *wind up* — the same, more informal; *turn out* — happen or prove to be in the end; *land in* — informal, end up in a bad place or situation.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To prove to be true in the end, or to happen or develop in a particular way.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and storytelling, with no object in this sense. Common patterns are *turn out (to be) + noun / adjective*, *it turns out (that) …* for surprising news, and *turn out well / fine / badly* for results. *As it turns out* introduces a fact that changes the situation.
entries.pattern: turn out (to be) …; it turns out (that) …; turn out well / badly
examples: The "quick fix" **turned out** to be a three-day job.
It **turns out** that my new neighbor used to be my sister's piano teacher.
I was nervous about baking my first cake, but it **turned out** great.

drill.sentence: We were worried about the rain all week, but the family reunion {{turned out}} perfectly.
drill.hint: happened, in the end (not *went* or *worked out*)

entries.related: *end up* — finally be in an unplanned situation; *work out* — end successfully; *pan out* — informal, develop as hoped, often in the negative.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To tell someone a fact or draw their attention to something, often a problem or something they missed.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, meetings and writing: *point out a mistake*, *point out that …*. It is separable with short noun objects, but a pronoun must go in the middle (*point it out*), and with a *that*-clause *out* comes first. The person you tell follows *to*: *point it out to her*.
entries.pattern: point out + a mistake / a problem / that …; point it out (to someone)
examples: My editor **pointed out** that I'd used the word "amazing" six times on one page.
As we drove through town, my dad **pointed out** the house where he grew up.
If you notice a typo in the menu, please **point it out** before we send it to the printer.

drill.sentence: I didn't want to embarrass her, so I waited until we were alone to {{point out}} the spinach in her teeth.
drill.hint: draw her attention to (not *mention*)

entries.related: *mention* — say briefly, without stressing it; *highlight* — make something stand out as important; *point someone out* — show which person in a group you mean.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To mention a subject so that people start discussing it.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and meetings, often for sensitive or awkward topics. It is separable: *bring up the issue* or *bring the issue up*, but always *bring it up* with a pronoun. It also means raising a child: *She was brought up by her grandparents.*
entries.pattern: bring up + a subject / an issue (with someone); bring it up
examples: Every time I **bring up** money, my husband finds a reason to leave the room.
Please don't **bring up** his ex at the party; he's still upset about the breakup.
Several parents **brought up** the issue of late school buses at the meeting.

drill.sentence: I wanted to ask my boss for Friday off, but he was in such a bad mood that I didn't {{bring it up}}.
drill.hint: start talking about the subject (pronoun in the middle; not *mention* or *raise*)

entries.related: *raise* — more formal, *raise an issue*; *come up* — the subject itself is mentioned; *broach* — formal, carefully start talking about a difficult subject.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To investigate a problem, question or complaint in order to find out the facts.
entries.usage: Very common at work and in customer service: *I'll look into it and get back to you.* It is inseparable: the object always follows *into*, even a pronoun (*look into it*). *We're looking into it* is a standard official reply that promises action without promising a result.
entries.pattern: look into + problem / complaint / question / possibility
examples: The airline promised to **look into** why my suitcase ended up in Denver.
The city is **looking into** why the water on our street keeps turning brown.
We're **looking into** adopting a second dog, but we haven't decided yet.

drill.sentence: My card was charged twice for the same dinner, and the bank promised to {{look into}} it and tell me what went wrong.
drill.hint: find out the facts about (phrasal verb; not *deal with*)

entries.related: *investigate* — more formal; *check into* — informal American, very similar; *dig into* — informal, look deeply into something.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To delay doing something until a later time, often because it is unpleasant or inconvenient.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often with *keep* + *-ing* for a habit of delaying: *I keep putting it off.* It is followed by a noun or *-ing*, never *to* + verb, and it is separable: *put the meeting off*, *put it off*. *Put someone off* is a different sense: make them dislike something.
entries.pattern: put off + noun / -ing (until + time); put it off
examples: I've been **putting off** cleaning the garage for months.
They **put the wedding off** until next spring because of her father's surgery.
Don't **put it off** any longer; your taxes are due on Friday.

drill.sentence: She kept {{putting off}} going to the dentist until the toothache got so bad she couldn't sleep.
drill.hint: delaying, because it seemed unpleasant (phrasal verb)

mistake.wrong: I keep putting off to call my grandmother.
mistake.right: I keep putting off calling my grandmother.
mistake.why: *Put off* is followed by *-ing*, not by *to* + verb.

entries.related: *postpone* — more formal, for events; *push back* — informal, move to a later time; *procrastinate* — delay things as a habit.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To establish or arrange something, such as a company, a meeting or a system, and get it ready to work.
entries.usage: Very common at work and at home: *set up a meeting, a business, an account, a tent, a printer*. It is separable: *set the tent up*, and always *set it up* with a pronoun. The noun is written as one word: *the setup*.
entries.pattern: set up + meeting / company / account / equipment; set it up
examples: My sister **set up** her own cleaning business when she was only twenty-three.
Can you help me **set up** the new TV? I can't get it to connect to the Wi-Fi.
Let's **set up** a call next week to talk about the move.

drill.sentence: We got to the campsite after dark and had to {{set up}} the tent using our phones as flashlights.
drill.hint: put together and make ready (not *put up* or *pitch*)

entries.related: *establish* — formal, for organizations; *arrange* — plan a meeting or event; *set someone up* — trick someone, or arrange a date for them.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To accept a job, task or responsibility, especially a difficult or extra one.
entries.usage: Common at work and in daily life: *take on a project, extra work, new clients*. It is separable: *take on more work* or *take more work on*, and always *take it on*. It often comes with *too much*: *I've taken on too much this month.*
entries.pattern: take on + a job / a project / responsibility / too much
examples: She **took on** a second job to pay for her daughter's braces.
Few law firms wanted the case, but a young lawyer agreed to **take it on** for free.
I've **taken on** too much this semester, and I'm barely sleeping.

drill.sentence: I'd love to help with the fundraiser, but I can't {{take on}} anything else this month; I'm already working weekends.
drill.hint: accept as an extra responsibility (not *handle*)

entries.related: *take over* — take control from someone else; *take someone on* — compete against or hire them; *bite off more than you can chew* — take on too much.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To take control of something, such as a company or a task, or to take responsibility for something from someone else.
entries.usage: Used without an object (*Can you take over while I make a call?*), with *from* + the person replaced, or with an object: *take over a company*. With an object it is separable, and a pronoun must go in the middle: *take it over*. The noun is one word: *a takeover*.
entries.pattern: take over (from + someone); take over + company / role / task
examples: When the chef retired, his daughter **took over** the restaurant.
I'm exhausted from driving; can you **take over** for a while?
Weeds have completely **taken over** the backyard since we stopped gardening.

drill.sentence: Ana Rivera will {{take over}} from Tom Chen as principal when he retires in June.
drill.hint: assume the role (phrasal verb, followed here by *from*)

entries.related: *take on* — accept a task; *step in* — help or replace someone, often in an emergency; *hand over* — the opposite, give control to someone else.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To experience a difficult or unpleasant period or event.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation about divorce, illness, grief and hard times: *She's going through a lot right now.* It is inseparable: the experience always follows *through*. *Go through* also means checking something carefully (*go through the paperwork*), so the object shows which sense is meant.
entries.pattern: go through + a divorce / a hard time / a lot / a phase
examples: He's **going through** a divorce, so be patient if he seems distracted.
Every teenager **goes through** a phase of hating their parents' music.
Nobody should have to **go through** chemotherapy alone.

drill.sentence: My best friend was amazing when I was {{going through}} a hard time after my father died.
drill.hint: experiencing a painful period (phrasal verb; not *having*)

entries.related: *get through* — survive or finish a hard period; *undergo* — formal, for medical treatment or change; *live through* — survive a long or historic hardship.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To refuse an offer, request or invitation.
entries.usage: Very common and neutral: *turn down a job, an offer, an invitation, a request*. It is separable: *turned the offer down*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *turned it down*. With a person as object it means rejecting them, often romantically: *She turned him down.*
entries.pattern: turn down + offer / invitation / job / request; turn someone down
examples: She **turned down** a job in Paris because she didn't want to leave her parents.
I finally asked her to prom, and she **turned me down**.
The city **turned down** the developer's request to build a twelve-story hotel by the beach.

drill.sentence: They offered me a raise to stay, but I {{turned it down}} because I'd already accepted the other job.
drill.hint: said no to the offer (phrasal verb; pronoun in the middle)

entries.related: *decline* — more formal and polite; *reject* — stronger, often about applications or ideas; *turn down the music* — the literal sense, lower the volume.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To develop in a good way or be successful in the end.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often to reassure someone (*It'll all work out*) or to say that a plan or relationship failed: *It didn't work out.* In this sense it has no object; the subject is the plan, situation or relationship. In other senses it means *exercise* or, with an object, *solve* or *calculate*.
entries.pattern: something works out (well / for the best); it didn't work out
examples: We were together for three years, but it just didn't **work out**.
Moving to Denver was a gamble, but it **worked out** well for the whole family.
Don't stress about finding a new roommate; I'm sure it'll all **work out**.

drill.sentence: My cousin opened a food truck last year, but it didn't {{work out}}, so he's back at his old job.
drill.hint: end successfully (not *pan out*, *take off* or *go well*)

entries.related: *pan out* — informal, develop as hoped; *turn out* — happen in the end, well or badly; *fall through* — fail to happen, about plans and deals.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be mentioned or discussed in a conversation or meeting, often without being planned.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and at work. It has no object: the topic is the subject, and *in* or *during* gives the setting (*Her name came up in the meeting*). It also means *happen unexpectedly*, as in the common excuse *Something came up, so I can't make it.*
entries.pattern: a topic / name / question + comes up (in / during + conversation / meeting)
examples: Your name **came up** at dinner last night; my brother says you two went to the same college.
The question of who pays for parking **came up** at every neighborhood meeting.
If the subject of salary **comes up** in the interview, be ready with a number.

drill.sentence: We were talking about old movies when, somehow, my uncle's army stories {{came up}}.
drill.hint: got mentioned (phrasal verb; not *popped up*)

entries.related: *bring something up* — mention a topic yourself; *crop up* — appear unexpectedly, usually a problem; *arise* — formal, happen or appear.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To recover from an illness, a shock, a loss or a disappointment, so that it no longer affects you.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation: *get over a cold, a breakup, the shock*. It is inseparable: the thing always follows *over*, even a pronoun (*get over it*). *Get over it!* is a rude way to tell someone to stop complaining, and *I can't get over …* expresses surprise: *I can't get over how tall you are!*
entries.pattern: get over + illness / breakup / shock / disappointment; get over it
examples: It took me months to **get over** the breakup.
She's still **getting over** the flu, so she won't be at practice this week.
The team never really **got over** losing the championship in overtime.

drill.sentence: My aunt never fully {{got over}} the death of her dog; she still keeps his collar by the front door.
drill.hint: recovered emotionally from (phrasal verb; not *moved on from*)

entries.related: *recover from* — more formal, often medical; *move on* — stop focusing on the past; *bounce back* — recover quickly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To accept or tolerate something or someone unpleasant without complaining, often because you cannot change it.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, usually about noise, bad behavior, pain or difficult people. It is inseparable: the object always follows *with*, even a pronoun (*put up with him*). It often appears with *have to*, *can't* or *won't*: *I won't put up with this.*
entries.pattern: put up with + noise / behavior / someone; won't put up with it
examples: I don't know how you **put up with** that noise every night.
My roommate leaves dirty dishes in the sink for days, but I **put up with** it because she always pays her rent on time.
The teacher made it clear she wouldn't **put up with** phones in class.

drill.sentence: The commute is long and the train is always crowded, but I {{put up with}} it because I love my job.
drill.hint: tolerate without complaining (three words; not *deal with* or *live with*)

entries.related: *tolerate* — more formal; *deal with* — handle a problem actively; *stand* — usually negative, *I can't stand it*.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To meet someone you know by chance, without planning it.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation: *I ran into your mom at the grocery store.* It is inseparable: the person always follows *into*, even a pronoun (*ran into her*). *Run into* can also mean hit something while driving (*ran into a tree*) or meet problems (*run into trouble*).
entries.pattern: run into + someone (at / in + place)
examples: I **ran into** my old high school coach at the airport, and we talked for an hour.
You'll never guess who I **ran into** at the farmers market this morning.
In a town this small, you can't go to the store without **running into** someone you know.

drill.sentence: I was wearing my oldest sweatpants, so of course that's the day I {{ran into}} my ex at the coffee shop.
drill.hint: met by chance (not *bumped into*)

entries.related: *bump into* — the same, equally common; *come across* — find something or someone by chance; *catch up with* — meet and talk after a long time.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To rely on someone to help you or to do what they promised.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work, especially as a promise: *You can count on me.* It is inseparable: the person follows *on*, and *to* + verb gives the action (*count on her to help*). It also works with things, often in the negative: *Don't count on it.*
entries.pattern: count on + someone (to + verb / for + something)
examples: My neighbor is the one person I can always **count on** to feed the cat when I travel.
The coach knew he could **count on** his goalie in a shootout.
Don't **count on** the bus being on time; leave early.

drill.sentence: My brother says he'll help, but you can't {{count on}} him; he cancels half the time.
drill.hint: trust to deliver what he promised (verb + *on*; not *rely* or *depend*)

entries.related: *rely on* — the same, a bit more formal; *depend on* — similar, also means *be decided by*; *let someone down* — the opposite, fail to do what they expected.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To decide that something is impossible, not suitable or not the cause, so you stop considering it.
entries.usage: Common in news, medicine, police work and planning: *rule out a cause, an option, a date*. It is separable: *rule out Florida* or *rule Florida out*, and a pronoun goes in the middle (*rule it out*). *I wouldn't rule it out* means it is still possible.
entries.pattern: rule out + option / cause / possibility; I wouldn't rule it out
examples: The doctor ordered an X-ray to **rule out** a broken bone.
We've **ruled out** Florida for our vacation; it's just too hot in August.
Investigators haven't **ruled out** a gas leak as the cause of the explosion.

drill.sentence: The mechanic {{ruled out}} the battery, since the lights and radio still worked fine.
drill.hint: decided it couldn't be the cause (phrasal verb; not *crossed off*)

entries.related: *eliminate* — more formal; *exclude* — leave out of a group or list; *consider* — the opposite, keep as a possibility.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To support someone, or to confirm that what they say is true.
entries.usage: Very common at work and among friends: *Will you back me up in the meeting?* It is separable, and a pronoun must go in the middle: *back me up*, *back her up*. Evidence can also *back up* a claim or story; the one-word noun *backup* means support or a copy of data.
entries.pattern: back someone up (on + point); back up + claim / story
examples: If my mom asks, will you **back me up** and say I was at your house?
When the customer started yelling, my manager came over and **backed me up**.
Several witnesses **backed up** her story about the accident.

drill.sentence: When I told Mom that my little brother broke the lamp, my sister {{backed me up}}.
drill.hint: confirmed what I said (pronoun in the middle; not *supported* or *stood up for*)

entries.related: *stand up for* — defend someone who is attacked; *have someone's back* — informal, be ready to support them; *vouch for* — say that someone is honest or reliable.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To arrive somewhere, especially where people are expecting you.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation: *show up late*, *show up for work*, *not show up at all*. It has no object; *at* or *to* introduces the place or event (*show up to the party*). It often suggests the arrival was uncertain or surprising, and a *no-show* is someone who never comes.
entries.pattern: show up (late / early) (at / to / for + event)
examples: We invited forty people, but only twelve **showed up**.
He **showed up** to the interview twenty minutes late and without a résumé.
My sister **showed up** at my door at midnight with a suitcase and a bag of tacos.

drill.sentence: The plumber said he'd come at nine, but he didn't {{show up}} until after lunch.
drill.hint: appear where you are expected (two words; not *turn up*)

entries.related: *turn up* — the same, more common in British English; *drop by* — visit briefly and casually; *no-show* — a person who does not come.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To use all of something so that none is left.
entries.usage: Very common for time, money, gas, patience, ideas and supplies. The person or place is the subject (*We ran out of milk*); without *of*, the thing itself is the subject (*The milk ran out*). It is inseparable: the thing always follows *of*.
entries.pattern: run out of + time / money / gas / patience; something runs out
examples: We **ran out of** gas ten miles from the nearest town.
Sorry, we **ran out of** the chocolate cake an hour ago. Can I get you the cheesecake instead?
I'm **running out of** patience with this airline.

drill.sentence: The printer {{ran out of}} ink right in the middle of printing our boarding passes.
drill.hint: had none left of (phrasal verb; not the one with *low*)

entries.related: *run low on* — have only a little left; *use up* — use all of something; *be out of* — have none at the moment.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To move or make progress at the same speed as others, so that you do not fall behind.
entries.usage: Common for walking, running, school, work and fast change: *keep up with the class, demand, the news*. It is inseparable: the person or thing follows *with*. Without an object, *keep up* is also common: *Slow down, I can't keep up!*
entries.pattern: keep up with + someone / the class / demand / the news
examples: My grandfather walks so fast that I can barely **keep up with** him.
The bakery can't bake fast enough to **keep up with** demand on weekends.
She missed two weeks of school and is struggling to **keep up with** the rest of the class.

drill.sentence: Our new puppy has so much energy that the kids can't {{keep up with}} her on walks.
drill.hint: go as fast as (not the form with *pace*)

entries.related: *keep pace with* — the same, more formal; *catch up with* — reach someone who was ahead; *fall behind* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To keep following a plan, rule, decision or promise without changing it.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about diets, budgets, schedules and rules: *stick to the plan, a budget, the rules*. It is inseparable: the object always follows *to*. It can also mean limit yourself to one thing: *I'll stick to water tonight.*
entries.pattern: stick to + plan / budget / diet / rules / schedule
examples: If we **stick to** the budget this month, we can afford a weekend at the lake.
My doctor says the diet only works if I **stick to** it.
The referee **stuck to** the rules, even though the home crowd booed him.

drill.sentence: We said we'd leave at six to beat the traffic, so let's {{stick to}} the plan, even if it means skipping breakfast.
drill.hint: keep following without changing (verb + *to*; not *keep to*)

entries.related: *stick with* — keep doing or using something, or stay loyal to someone; *keep to* — the same, more British; *deviate from* — formal, the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To find or meet something or someone by chance, without looking for it.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and writing about things you find while reading, cleaning or browsing: *come across an article, an old photo, a new word*. It is inseparable: the thing always follows *across*, even a pronoun (*came across it*). *Come across as* is a different meaning: seem (*He comes across as shy*).
entries.pattern: come across + article / photo / word / place
examples: While cleaning the attic, I **came across** a box of letters my grandparents wrote to each other.
If you **come across** a good recipe for vegan lasagna, send it my way.
I've never **come across** anyone as stubborn as my four-year-old.

drill.sentence: I {{came across}} this tiny bookstore by accident when I took a wrong turn downtown.
drill.hint: found by chance (not *stumbled on*)

entries.related: *stumble on* — find by chance, often something important; *run into* — meet a person by chance; *come across as* — seem to be.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To agree to or accept a plan, idea or decision, often without really wanting to or without arguing.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work. It often suggests passive agreement: you accept something to avoid conflict, not because you love it (*I just went along with it*). It is inseparable: the object follows *with*, and it can also be a person: *go along with your boss*.
entries.pattern: go along with + plan / idea / decision / someone
examples: I didn't love the idea of camping in November, but I **went along with** it to keep the peace.
The board **went along with** the CEO's plan, even though several members had doubts.
Kids often **go along with** a dare because they don't want to look scared.

drill.sentence: Everyone else wanted pizza, so I {{went along with}} it, even though I'd been craving sushi all day.
drill.hint: accepted, without arguing (three words; not *agreed to*)

entries.related: *agree to* — accept a request or plan; *play along* — pretend to agree or cooperate; *object to* — the opposite, say you are against it.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To review or check something carefully, step by step, often with someone else.
entries.usage: Very common at work, in school and before important events: *go over the plan, the numbers, your notes*. In this meaning it is inseparable: the object follows *over*, even a pronoun (*Let's go over it again*). *Go over something with someone* means review it together.
entries.pattern: go over + plan / notes / numbers / details (with someone)
examples: Before the wedding, the planner **went over** the schedule with us minute by minute.
Let's **go over** your answers before you hand in the test.
My accountant **went over** our receipts and found three hundred dollars in extra deductions.

drill.sentence: The night before her driving test, my dad {{went over}} the rules for four-way stops with her one more time.
drill.hint: reviewed step by step (not the form with *through*)

entries.related: *go through* — very close, often more thorough or line by line; *review* — more formal; *look over* — check quickly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To reply to someone later, by phone, email or message, usually with information they asked for.
entries.usage: Extremely common in work emails and calls (*I'll get back to you by Friday*), often as a polite way to delay an answer. The person follows *to*, and *on* or *about* gives the topic: *get back to you on the price*. *Get back to* + a task means return to it: *get back to work*.
entries.pattern: get back to + someone (on / about + topic) (by + time)
examples: I'll check my calendar and **get back to** you by the end of the day.
The landlord still hasn't **gotten back to** me about the broken window.
Thanks for the offer; can I **get back to** you after I talk to my wife?

drill.sentence: The doctor's office said they'd {{get back to}} me with my test results by Friday, but I still haven't heard anything.
drill.hint: reply later to (phrasal verb; not *contact* or *call*)

entries.related: *follow up* — contact someone again about something discussed; *call someone back* — return a phone call; *hear back from someone* — receive their reply.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To do a task, plan, study or order, especially an official or planned one.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal and very common in reports, news and instructions: *carry out a study, a plan, repairs, an order, a threat*. With a noun object, *out* usually comes first (*carry out the plan*), but a pronoun goes in the middle: *carry it out*. In casual speech people often just say *do*.
entries.pattern: carry out + study / plan / repairs / order / threat
examples: The city will **carry out** repairs on the bridge over the summer.
It's a great plan on paper, but who's actually going to **carry it out**?
Researchers **carried out** the study in three hospitals over two years.

drill.sentence: The family hired a contractor to {{carry out}} the renovation while they stayed with relatives.
drill.hint: perform the work of (phrasal verb; not *take on*)

entries.related: *conduct* — formal, for studies and surveys; *implement* — formal, put a plan or decision into action; *follow through on* — finish what you promised or started.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To invent a story, excuse or explanation that is not true.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often as an accusation: *Did you just make that up?* It is separable: *make up an excuse* or *make an excuse up*, and always *make it up* with a pronoun. It can also mean inventing for fun, as with songs or bedtime stories.
entries.pattern: make up + a story / an excuse / a name; make it up
examples: He **made up** a story about a flat tire, but we found out he'd just overslept.
My dad used to **make up** bedtime stories about a dragon who was afraid of the dark.
Some of the reviews on the site were clearly **made up** by the owner's friends.

drill.sentence: I didn't want to go to the party, so I {{made up}} an excuse about having to babysit my nephew.
drill.hint: created something untrue (phrasal verb; not *came up with* or *thought up*)

entries.related: *come up with* — think of an idea, true or not; *fabricate* — formal, invent false information; *make up for* — a different verb: compensate for something.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To do something good to balance something bad, or to replace something that was lost or missed.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports and apologies: *make up for lost time*, *make up for a mistake*. It is inseparable: the thing follows *for*, even a pronoun (*make up for it*). *Make it up to someone* is a related pattern: do something nice for a person you disappointed.
entries.pattern: make up for + mistake / lost time / lack of something
examples: Sorry I missed your recital; I'll come to both shows next week to **make up for** it.
What the restaurant lacks in decor, it **makes up for** in flavor.
After years of working weekends, she's **making up for** lost time with her kids.

drill.sentence: We lost the first game badly, but we {{made up for}} it with a big win the next weekend.
drill.hint: balanced out the loss (phrasal verb with *for*; not *compensated*)

entries.related: *compensate for* — formal; *make amends* — do something to show you are sorry; *make up* — a different verb: invent a story, or end an argument.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop thinking about a past event or relationship and start something new.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation about breakups, jobs, mistakes and loss: *It's time to move on.* It has no direct object; *from* gives the past thing and *to* gives the next one. In meetings it also means change to the next topic: *Let's move on.*
entries.pattern: move on (from + past event / to + next thing)
examples: It's been two years since the divorce; I think he's finally ready to **move on**.
After eight years at the same firm, she felt it was time to **move on** to something new.
The team needs to **move on** from last week's loss and focus on Sunday's game.

drill.sentence: I know you're still upset about the argument, but she apologized, so it's time to {{move on}}.
drill.hint: leave the past behind (phrasal verb; not *let it go* or *get over it*)

entries.related: *get over* — recover from something painful; *let go* — stop holding on emotionally; *dwell on* — the opposite, keep thinking about the past.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To deal successfully with a difficult situation or problem, so that you can keep going.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, health writing and news: *cope with stress, grief, pain, pressure, demand*. *Cope* can also stand alone (*How are you coping?*), and *with* introduces the problem. It suggests getting through difficulty, not necessarily solving it.
entries.pattern: cope with + stress / grief / pressure / demand; how are you coping?
examples: Many new parents struggle to **cope with** the lack of sleep.
Running is how I **cope with** stress at work.
The hospital couldn't **cope with** the number of patients during the heat wave.

drill.sentence: After her husband died, she joined a support group to help her {{cope with}} the grief.
drill.hint: manage emotionally (verb + *with*; not *deal with*)

entries.related: *deal with* — handle a problem, more general; *get through* — survive a hard period; *struggle with* — have great difficulty with.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To manage to survive or finish something difficult, unpleasant or long.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about hard periods, tasks and events: *get through the winter, a tough week, an exam, a pile of work*. In this meaning it is inseparable: the thing follows *through*, even a pronoun (*We'll get through this*). *Get through to someone* is a different verb: make them understand, or reach them by phone.
entries.pattern: get through + a hard time / the day / the week / an exam
examples: I don't know how we'll **get through** the winter with heating bills this high.
Coffee and loud music are how I **get through** Monday mornings.
She **got through** the funeral without crying, then broke down in the car.

drill.sentence: It's been a terrible year for our family, but we'll {{get through}} it together, like we always do.
drill.hint: survive to the end of (phrasal verb; not the one with *make it*)

entries.related: *make it through* — the same, stressing success; *pull through* — recover from a serious illness; *go through* — experience something hard, without saying you survived it.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To fail to keep up with others or with a schedule, so that you do less than expected or needed.
entries.usage: Common for school, work, payments and races. Use *on* for payments and work (*fall behind on rent*), *in* for a subject (*fall behind in math*), and a direct object for people or schedules: *fall behind the others*, *fall behind schedule*. *Get behind* is a casual equivalent.
entries.pattern: fall behind (on + rent / work; in + class; + schedule / the others)
examples: After she lost her job, she **fell behind** on her rent and got an eviction notice.
He missed a month of school with mono and **fell behind** in math.
The runner **fell behind** the lead group after the twentieth mile.

drill.sentence: The construction crew {{fell behind}} schedule because of all the rain, so the school won't open until October.
drill.hint: failed to keep up with (the verb is not *got* or *ran*)

entries.related: *keep up with* — the opposite, stay at the same speed; *catch up* — reach others after being behind; *lag behind* — move or develop more slowly than others.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be easy to notice, or to be clearly better or more impressive than others.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, job advice and reviews: *make your résumé stand out*, *stand out from the crowd*. It has no object; *from* or *among* introduces the others. The one-word adjective *standout* means excellent: *the standout dish of the night*.
entries.pattern: stand out (from / among + others); make something stand out
examples: In his bright orange jacket, he really **stood out** in the crowd.
Of all the applicants, one **stood out**: she'd built her own robot in high school.
Add a short personal story to your cover letter to make it **stand out**.

drill.sentence: She was the only one in the choir with such a deep voice, so she always {{stood out}} at concerts.
drill.hint: was easy to notice (phrasal verb; not *stuck out*)

entries.related: *stick out* — be very noticeable, often in a bad way; *blend in* — the opposite, look like everyone else; *outshine* — be much better than others.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To feel accepted and comfortable as part of a group, because you are similar to the others or get along with them.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation about school, new jobs, neighborhoods and families: *I never really fit in.* It has no object in this meaning; *with* introduces the group (*fit in with the other kids*). In American English the past tense is usually *fit*, not *fitted*.
entries.pattern: fit in (with + group / at + place)
examples: As the only kid from out of state, I didn't **fit in** at first.
Our new coworker **fits in** perfectly; she even laughs at Steve's terrible jokes.
Teenagers will do almost anything to **fit in** with their friends.

drill.sentence: We worried our shy son would struggle at his new school, but he {{fit in}} right away and made lots of friends.
drill.hint: was accepted by the group (phrasal verb; not *settled in*)

entries.related: *settle in* — get used to a new place; *belong* — feel that you are part of a group; *out of place* — the opposite, not comfortable in a situation.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To lose the chance to have or enjoy something good, often because you were not there or did not act in time.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and ads: *Don't miss out!* Use *miss out on* + noun or *-ing* to name what you lose; *miss out* also stands alone. The noun *FOMO* (*fear of missing out*) comes from it.
entries.pattern: miss out (on + noun / -ing)
examples: I had the flu during the class trip, so I **missed out** on the whole week in Washington.
We got to the bakery at noon and **missed out** on the famous cinnamon rolls; they sell out by ten.
He works so much that he feels he's **missing out** on his kids growing up.

drill.sentence: Everyone was talking about the concert on Monday, and I felt like I'd really {{missed out}}.
drill.hint: lost the chance to enjoy something good (phrasal verb; not *lost out*)

entries.related: *lose out* — be at a disadvantage, often to someone else; *miss the boat* — miss a chance by being too slow; *FOMO* — informal, fear of missing out.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To disappoint someone by not doing what they hoped or expected, or what you promised.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports and apologies: *I'm sorry I let you down.* The person usually goes in the middle (*let the team down*), and a pronoun must: *let me down*. The one-word noun *letdown* means a disappointment: *The movie was a real letdown.*
entries.pattern: let someone down; let the team / your family down
examples: She promised to help with the move and never came; she really **let me down**.
The kicker felt he'd **let the whole team down** after missing the field goal.
Don't worry, I won't **let you down**; the cake will be ready by noon.

drill.sentence: My parents were counting on me to finish college, and I didn't want to {{let them down}}.
drill.hint: fail to meet their hopes (phrasal verb; pronoun in the middle)

mistake.wrong: I'm sorry, I didn't want to let down you.
mistake.right: I'm sorry, I didn't want to let you down.
mistake.why: With a separable phrasal verb, a pronoun object must go between the verb and the particle.

entries.related: *disappoint* — more formal; *fail someone* — stronger, not give the help you should; *come through for someone* — the opposite, do what they needed.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be as good as people expected or hoped, or to do what you promised.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, sports and conversation: *live up to the hype, expectations, its reputation, a promise*. It is inseparable: the standard always follows *to*. It is often negative: *The sequel didn't live up to the original.*
entries.pattern: live up to + expectations / the hype / a reputation / a promise
examples: Everyone raved about the new taco place, but it didn't **live up to** the hype.
As the son of a famous coach, he always felt pressure to **live up to** his father's name.
The hotel **lived up to** its reputation: spotless rooms and an amazing breakfast.

drill.sentence: Her first novel was a huge hit, so the second one had a lot to {{live up to}}.
drill.hint: be as good as (phrasal verb)

entries.related: *meet expectations* — more formal; *fall short of* — the opposite, not be good enough; *exceed expectations* — be better than expected.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To bring good results after a lot of effort, time or risk.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, sports and business: *All that practice paid off.* In this sense it has no object; the subject is the effort, risk or investment. With an object, *pay off* means pay a debt completely (*pay off a loan*, *pay it off*), and that use is separable.
entries.pattern: hard work / practice / a risk + pays off
examples: All those early-morning practices finally **paid off** when the team won the state title.
Our gamble on a smaller apartment closer to work **paid off**; we save two hours a day.
Learning some Spanish before the trip really **paid off** in the small villages.

drill.sentence: She studied every weekend for six months, and it {{paid off}}: she passed the bar exam on her first try.
drill.hint: brought the hoped-for result (phrasal verb; not *was worth it*)

entries.related: *be worth it* — justify the cost or effort; *bear fruit* — formal, finally produce results; *backfire* — the opposite, have a bad result.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To reduce the amount of something you use, eat, buy or spend.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about health and money: *cut back on sugar, coffee, spending, screen time*. *Cut back* can also stand alone (*We're trying to cut back*), and *cut down on* means almost the same. It is inseparable: the thing follows *on*.
entries.pattern: cut back on + sugar / coffee / spending / hours
examples: My doctor told me to **cut back on** salt, so I've stopped eating chips.
We're **cutting back on** eating out until we've paid off the credit card.
The factory **cut back on** overtime after orders dropped.

drill.sentence: I'm trying to {{cut back on}} coffee, so I only have one cup in the morning now.
drill.hint: reduce how much I drink of (not the form with *down*)

entries.related: *cut down on* — the same; *give up* — stop completely; *scale back* — reduce the size of a plan or project.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To do something you did not have time to do earlier, such as sleep, work or reading.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about sleep, email, work, reading and TV shows: *catch up on sleep*, *catch up on the news*. It is inseparable: the thing follows *on*. *Catch up* alone means reach someone who is ahead, or talk with a friend you have not seen for a while.
entries.pattern: catch up on + sleep / work / email / reading / a show
examples: I spent Sunday **catching up on** sleep after a week of night shifts.
Now that the kids are at camp, I can finally **catch up on** my reading.
Let's stay in tonight and **catch up on** the show we stopped watching in March.

drill.sentence: I was sick for a week, so I'm staying late at the office to {{catch up on}} all the work I missed.
drill.hint: deal with the backlog of (not *make up*)

entries.related: *catch up* — talk about recent news with a friend; *make up* — do missed schoolwork or a test later; *fall behind* — the opposite, get behind.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To talk with someone about what has happened in your lives since you last met.
entries.usage: Very common and friendly in American conversation: *We should get together and catch up!* It has no direct object; *with* introduces the person (*catch up with an old friend*). Don't confuse it with *catch up on* (do what you missed) or with *catch up* meaning reach someone who is ahead: *Go ahead, I'll catch up.*
entries.pattern: catch up (with + someone) (over coffee / lunch)
examples: I hadn't seen Maria since college, so we met for lunch and spent three hours **catching up**.
Let's grab a coffee next week and **catch up**.
At the reunion, I barely had time to **catch up with** everyone before the band started.

drill.sentence: My cousin and I live on opposite coasts, so we video chat every Sunday to {{catch up}}.
drill.hint: share what's new in our lives (phrasal verb; not *keep in touch*)

entries.related: *keep in touch* — stay in contact over time; *touch base* — make brief contact, mostly at work; *catch up on* — do something you had no time for earlier.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To consider all the possible effects and problems of something carefully before you decide or act.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and advice, often as a criticism: *You didn't think this through, did you?* It is separable; the object usually goes in the middle (*think it through*, *think the plan through*), but *think through the consequences* is also used. A careful plan is *well-thought-out*.
entries.pattern: think it / the plan through; think through the consequences
examples: Before you quit your job, **think it through**: do you have enough savings for six months?
The new parking rules weren't **thought through**, and now nobody can find a spot downtown.
We **thought through** every detail of the surprise party, except where to hide forty guests.

drill.sentence: Buying a house is a huge decision, so take a few weeks to {{think it through}} before you sign anything.
drill.hint: consider all the consequences (pronoun in the middle; not *mull over* or *sleep on*)

entries.related: *mull something over* — think about it slowly over time; *sleep on it* — wait until tomorrow to decide; *rush into* — the opposite, act without thinking.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To give a short summary of the main points of something.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, presentations and writing, especially as *To sum up, …* at the end. It is separable: *sum up the discussion* or *sum it up*. It also means describe someone or something briefly and accurately: *That sums him up perfectly.*
entries.pattern: sum up + the main points / the discussion; to sum up, …; that sums it up
examples: At the end of the meeting, the manager **summed up** what each team had agreed to do.
Cold, wet and expensive: that **sums up** our week in London pretty well.
If you had to **sum up** your childhood in one word, what would it be?

drill.sentence: The coach {{summed up}} the season in one sentence: we played hard, but we didn't play smart.
drill.hint: described briefly, giving the main point (phrasal verb; not *summarized*)

entries.related: *summarize* — the one-word, more formal verb; *in a nutshell* — in very few words; *recap* — repeat the main points, often at work or on TV.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To say clearly what you think, especially to defend someone or something or to object to something wrong.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, at work and in schools. Use *for* + the person you defend (*speak up for yourself*) and *about* or *against* + the problem. It also means *talk louder*: *Could you speak up a little?*
entries.pattern: speak up (for + someone / about + problem / against + something)
examples: If you think the plan is wrong, **speak up** now, not after we've spent the money.
Nobody **spoke up** when the new kid was being teased, and I still regret it.
My grandmother taught me to **speak up** for myself, even when it's uncomfortable.

drill.sentence: When the waiter was rude to my friend, the whole table was silent until my sister finally {{spoke up}}.
drill.hint: said clearly what she thought (phrasal verb; particle not *out*)

entries.related: *speak out* — protest publicly, often against injustice; *stand up for* — defend someone; *keep quiet* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start talking honestly about your feelings or private experiences.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about relationships, therapy and family, and in celebrity interviews: *She opened up about her divorce.* It has no object in this sense; *to* introduces the listener and *about* the topic. It suggests the person was quiet or private before.
entries.pattern: open up (to + someone) (about + experience / feelings)
examples: It took months of therapy before he **opened up** about his time in the army.
My daughter rarely talks about school, but she **opens up** on long car rides.
In the interview, the singer **opened up** about her struggle with anxiety.

drill.sentence: My dad never talked about his childhood, but last summer he finally {{opened up}} to me about it.
drill.hint: began to share his private feelings (phrasal verb; not *talked*)

entries.related: *confide in* — tell someone a secret; *pour your heart out* — tell all your feelings at once; *clam up* — the opposite, suddenly stop talking.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To defend or support someone or something that is being attacked or criticized.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, at school and at work: *stand up for yourself, a friend, your rights, what you believe in*. It is inseparable: the person or thing always follows *for*, even a pronoun (*stand up for her*). It suggests courage, often against someone more powerful.
entries.pattern: stand up for + someone / yourself / your rights / what you believe in
examples: When the other kids laughed at my accent, my best friend **stood up for** me.
You need to **stand up for** yourself; don't let your boss take credit for your work.
The whole town **stood up for** its library when the county planned to close it.

drill.sentence: When a man started yelling at the cashier, two other customers {{stood up for}} her.
drill.hint: took her side and defended her (not *stuck up for*)

entries.related: *stick up for* — the same, more informal; *back someone up* — support or confirm what they say; *speak up* — say what you think.
